intro: After three orchestral movements, an alto gives Mahler’s Second Symphony its first words in a setting of Des Knaben Wunderhorn. How do the solitary voice and hymn-like orchestral writing change the scale of the music?
question: How does one voice change the scale of a symphony?

sections.label: Closing declaration
sections.mNote: first stanza’s rising phrases extended through chromatic sequences and tremolo

cues.title: A single human voice
cues.text: This is the first sung movement of the Second Symphony. Mahler asks for “very solemn, but simple”; compare the scale of one vocal line with the orchestral writing around it.
cues.evidence: The score establishes the first vocal movement and the marking Sehr feierlich, aber schlicht; no vocal entrance is aligned here.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Voice and chorale
cues.text: The opening sets a solitary vocal phrase beside a brass chorale: a melody harmonised in measured, hymn-like chords. Compare the lengths of the phrases and the difference between a single line and several parts moving together.
cues.evidence: The score gives the opening voice-and-chorale design; increased relative level around 0:20 supports a broad contrast, not a brass entrance time.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A poem from 1808
cues.text: “Urlicht” appears in the second volume of Des Knaben Wunderhorn, published in Heidelberg in 1808 by Achim von Arnim and Clemens Brentano. Mahler uses its words for a newly composed song, not a transcription of a folk performance.
cues.evidence: Deutsches Textarchiv’s 1808 volume lists Urlicht; the Mahler Foundation documents Mahler’s setting.

cues.title: Summer at Steinbach
cues.text: An early orchestral manuscript of “Urlicht” ends with “Steinbach / 19 Juli 1893”. Mahler subsequently revised the orchestration for the Second Symphony; the song existed before he decided to include it there.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation describes Zweig MS 49, folio 6r, and Mahler’s 1895 letter to Hermann Behn about the song’s earlier existence.

cues.title: Listen beneath the voice
cues.text: Through the sustained vocal writing, follow the slower changes in the accompaniment. A held note need not mean that the harmony beneath it is standing still; the lower parts can give a long phrase its direction.
cues.evidence: This is a guide to the sustained voice-and-accompaniment texture, without identifying a particular chord or word at this time.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A narrative middle passage
cues.text: The middle passage brings more movement into the song’s broad phrasing. The poem includes an encounter with an angel on a road; compare the more active musical writing with the solemn manner of the opening.
cues.evidence: The text supplies the encounter; a strong audio change near 2:40 and more frequent attacks support the passage’s approximate position, not word timings.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Refusing the angel
cues.text: The poem’s speaker refuses to be turned away: “Ich bin von Gott und will wieder zu Gott!” — “I am from God and want to return to God.” The line is the traveller’s reply to the angel, not a request for permission.
cues.evidence: The German text is reproduced by the Mahler Foundation; the English wording here is a close translation, not a timed subtitle.

cues.title: A sustained crest
cues.text: The later part of the song contains a broad swell followed by a withdrawal. Follow the length of the phrase rather than looking for a quicker beat to explain the increase in intensity.
cues.evidence: The strongest five-second relative-level window falls near 3:50, followed by a marked reduction towards 4:00.

cues.title: The last broad swell
cues.text: The closing span makes another broad rise before receding. Listen to the harmony beneath the long notes: the decrease in level begins before the movement has reached its final cadence.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises across 4:15–4:25 and falls substantially by 4:35, while the recording continues for another 24 seconds.

cues.title: Before the choral finale
cues.text: This small vocal movement ends in D♭ major before the symphony’s much larger finale. Compare its restrained close with the scale promised by the title “Resurrection”: the chorus’s answer still lies ahead in the complete work.
cues.evidence: The score gives the closing key and the movement’s position before the finale; the recording’s relative level declines through its final passage.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

transitions.title: The hymn yields to a human sentence
transitions.how: The chorale establishes D♭ major before the alto resumes the poem. Its measured brass chords give way to a more flexible vocal sentence and quieter accompaniment: the bass still supports the home key, but chromatic inner parts unsettle the hymn’s diatonic simplicity as the words turn to human suffering. The voice does not introduce a new tempo or an unrelated tune. Its rising gestures extend the opening invocation, while the harmony becomes less settled beneath them.
transitions.evidence: The 1:04 section boundary follows A♭-centred pitch content near 1:00 and a quiet window at 1:05 before the level rises at 1:10. Lew Smoley’s Mahler Foundation listening guide describes the D♭ chorale and the more chromatic second and third lines of the first stanza. The boundary locates that change broadly, not a particular word or brass release.

transitions.title: The oboe finishes; the story moves
transitions.how: The alto leaves the first stanza’s cadence to the oboe, whose turning figure completes the sentence. The narrative middle then moves from the D♭-major world to its relative minor, B♭ minor. A lighter, more mobile clarinet figure replaces the chorale’s chordal tread; a solo violin develops the new material into a longer line. This is a change in the accompaniment’s pace and character, not simply a louder continuation of the hymn.
transitions.evidence: The 2:40 section boundary coincides with a strong analysis change and a rise from about −29 dB at 2:35 to −10.5 dB at 2:40. Smoley’s Mahler Foundation guide identifies the oboe’s cadential turn, the B♭-minor middle, clarinet figure and subsequent solo violin. Their individual entrances are not audio-aligned.

transitions.title: Rising harmony turns refusal into affirmation
transitions.how: The middle has travelled as far as A major rather than staying in B♭ minor. Mahler does not jump straight back to the opening chorale: rising chromatic harmonies and string tremolo carry the traveller’s refusal into the final declaration. The upward sequences recall the first stanza’s striving phrases, now sustained across a larger swell. D♭ major is the destination, not a chord already securely reached at the join; the orchestra will eventually supply the cadence after the singer has finished.
transitions.evidence: The 3:24 section boundary follows A-major estimates around 3:05–3:10; level rises after 3:20 towards the broad crest at 3:50. Smoley’s Mahler Foundation guide supplies the middle’s A-major excursion, rising chromatic sequence, tremolo and orchestral completion of the final D♭ cadence. Neither the declaration’s words nor a single modulation chord are timed here.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
